name: Knossos Palace
label: Knossos Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Central Court' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Central court' (way/1205581210): middle (70 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/24258942: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Knossos Palace' (292 m across).
notes: The Minoan palace complex, Crete's most visited archaeological site.

text.description: Knossos is the largest and best-known centre of the Minoan civilisation, and the palace on Kephala hill is the part most visitors come to photograph. The first palace was built around 1900 BC. After a major destruction around 1700 BC it was rebuilt on a grander scale, with a central court, monumental entrances, staircases and light wells. In 2025 Knossos was inscribed as part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site Minoan Palatial Centres. For a phone photo, the best place to start is the Central Court. This open rectangular courtyard is surrounded by palace walls and columns, so one frame can show how the whole complex is laid out. If you can reach the upper terrace looking down into the court, that gives the clearest view. Then walk down to the middle of the courtyard floor and look south towards Mount Juktas. Once you have the wide view, move in on details such as column bases, stone steps and the rhythm of shadows on the walls. If you have time, the South Propylaeum (the entrance front) is lovely in warm evening light. The Grand Staircase has repeating stone landings and columns that suit close-up pictures. Some interior rooms, such as the Throne Room, can only be seen from the doorway behind a rope, and flash is not allowed there. Go early if you can, to get fewer people in your shots.
text.geographic_location: Knossos lies in the southern part of Heraklion, on Kephala hill in the Kairatos river valley, about 5 km south of the historic centre. The palace is the main feature of the archaeological site.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stop is listed for this spot. The site is about 5 km south of the historic centre of Heraklion. Once inside the site, follow the visitor route towards the Central Court. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole courtyard and its surrounding walls into one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural look, and the telephoto or zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as columns and stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (upper terrace overlooking the court, then the courtyard floor at its centre). The open rectangular courtyard with the surrounding palace walls and columns, framed to show the layout of the whole complex. For the best views, head to the Central Court as a separate viewpoint: first the upper terrace looking down into the court if you can get there, then the courtyard floor at its centre. From the court the photo shows the open rectangular courtyard with the palace walls and columns around it, so the layout of the complex is easy to read. From the middle of the floor, look south towards Mount Juktas.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the courtyard floor in the lower third, with the walls and columns filling the middle and the sky or Mount Juktas above. Keep the phone level so the walls don't lean. For a second picture, try the South Propylaeum for the entrance front in evening light, or the Grand Staircase for repeating shapes and shadows.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest stone wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale stone keeps its detail in strong sun. Don't use flash in the interior rooms; it is banned there. If you want a panorama of the court, pan slowly and keep your arm steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the tour groups arrive. Late afternoon is also worth trying for warmer light.

text.access_note: Several of the best viewpoints are inside the archaeological site, so check the official site for current opening hours, tickets and any closures before you go.

name: Heraklion Archaeological Museum
label: Archaeological Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/250686961: the OpenStreetMap point 'Heraklion Archaeological Museum'.
notes: The main collection of Minoan art, including the Phaistos Disc.

text.description: The Heraklion Archaeological Museum is a calm, pale modernist building in Heraklion, and it is the main place to see Minoan art in Crete. It holds most of the finds from the palace at Knossos and from other Minoan sites on the island, with objects spanning about 5,500 years, from the Neolithic period to Roman times. The collection began in 1883. The present building was designed by Patroklos Karantinos in the 1930s and has stood up to earthquakes and wartime bombing. Its use of veined, multicoloured marble echoes the painted imitation marble of Minoan palaces, which makes the front a pleasing subject on its own. Outside, the clean lines and flat facade suit a phone well. Stand square on to the building, switch on the gridlines and line up the horizontals with the edge of the frame. The building is the subject at the phone icon on the map itself, so you do not need to walk far to find a good angle. Step back a little to fit more of the front in at the default lens (1x), or use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is narrow. Inside, some exhibits cannot be photographed, and signs are usually posted near them, so look for those before you raise your phone. The museum is a ticketed site, so check the official site before you go for current times and entry rules.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in Heraklion on the island of Crete.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or railway stops are listed for this spot. The phone icon on the map sits right at the museum. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the front. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot step back far enough to fit the building in.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the building's horizontal lines level with them. Hold the phone straight rather than tilting it upwards, so the walls do not lean inwards. Include a little of the pavement for scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the front of the building to focus, then slide the exposure slider down a touch if the pale walls look washed out against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go in the morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and the stone looks less flat. Check the official site for opening times.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed museum, and some exhibits cannot be photographed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Koules Fortress
label: Koules Fortress
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Koules' (5 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Koules' (node/6017941705): point; moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OSM N8524600212 (VENETIAN FORTRESS KOULES): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Venetian sea fortress at the end of the old harbour mole.

text.description:
Koules is the fortress that stands at the entrance to Heraklion's harbour, and it photographs best from the water's edge. The classic picture is taken from the harbour side, on the approach along the breakwater (the outer harbour mole). From there the fortress sits at the end of the view, with moored yachts and fishing boats in the foreground and the water all around it. The boats give the stone walls scale and a bit of colour, so the picture feels like a place rather than just a building.

Guides treat the breakwater as the best outside vantage point and recommend it for sunset, when golden light falls on the stone. Walk a little way along the mole before you start shooting, and move along it to try different arrangements of the boats in the foreground. Keep the fortress in the upper part of the frame and let the boats and water fill the lower part.

There is a second option inside the fortress. The rooftop gives wide views over the harbour, the fishing boats below and the city of Heraklion spreading out behind. The rooftop is inside the ticketed fortress, so admission is needed and opening hours change with the season. Check the current opening hours before you go. Photography inside is generally fine as long as you stay considerate of other visitors.
text.geographic_location: Koules stands at the mouth of Heraklion's harbour, at the end of the outer breakwater, next to the moored yachts and fishing boats of the harbour.
text.directions_text: Head for Heraklion's harbour area, then follow the breakwater out towards the fortress. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full scene of fortress, boats and water. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the boats and want more of them in the foreground. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (harbour side, from the approach along the breakwater (mole) toward the fortress). The fortress standing at the harbour entrance with moored yachts and fishing boats in the foreground, framed against the water. On the harbour side, on the approach along the breakwater (mole) towards the fortress.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the fortress on one of the upper lines, with the moored boats along the lower part of the frame. Keep the horizon level. For a different version, the rooftop inside the fortress gives wide harbour and city views, though you will need a ticket.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stone walls to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the sky and water keep their colour at sunset. Try a Live Photo, as the boats moving on the water can give you a nicer frame to pick afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, when the golden light falls on the stone.

text.access_note: Viewing the fortress from the breakwater approach is free; the rooftop is inside the ticketed fortress with seasonal opening hours, so check the current opening hours before you go.

name: Morosini Fountain
label: Morosini Fountain
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Morosini Fountain' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/12119943: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Lions Square' (100 m across).
notes: Venetian fountain with four lions on Lions Square.

text.description:
The Morosini Fountain stands in the middle of Lions Square, the busy main square of Heraklion's old town. Four stone lions support the main basin, and the locals simply call the monument "the Lions". The square's official name is Eleftheriou Venizelou Square, after the Cretan statesman Eleftherios Venizelos, but almost everyone uses the nickname. Both the square and the fountain go back to the Venetian era.

It photographs well because the detail is rich and close at hand. The lions, the carved basins and the bas-reliefs all reward a slow walk around the monument rather than a single snap from a distance. The cafes and old-town buildings around the square make a lively backdrop when you step back a little.

For the close-up view, stand at ground level beside the basin and shoot upwards towards the lions and the upper basin. Walk right round it to see the carved details up close. The fountain is not always running, so you may not get a shot with water. If you do see it flowing, it adds movement and sparkle to the stonework. The square is popular and can be crowded, so be patient and wait for a gap if you want a clean frame. For a wider view with the cafes and surrounding buildings, Eleftheriou Venizelou Square itself is a good alternative spot to step back to.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Heraklion's old town, in the middle of Lions Square (Eleftheriou Venizelou Square), surrounded by cafes and old buildings.
text.directions_text: There is no Underground, tram or station stop right at this spot, so start from the old town centre of Heraklion and head for Lions Square. The fountain is in the middle of the square, so once you arrive you cannot miss it. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for most shots, and switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you are close to the basin and want the whole fountain in the frame. A telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is handy for picking out lion faces and carved panels.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here, stand at ground level around the basin and aim up towards the lions and the upper basin. Walk all the way round to find the best side.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place a lion on one of the thirds, with the upper basin above it. Move in close for details of the bas-reliefs, then step back for a wider shot with the square around it. For a wider view of the whole fountain among the cafes and buildings, Eleftheriou Venizelou Square is a good alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then use the exposure slider to bring the brightness down slightly if the sky is washing out the top of the fountain. If the water is running, try a Live Photo to capture the movement.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the morning to avoid the crowds, as the square can be very busy, especially at weekends and in summer.

text.access_note: The fountain is a public monument in an open square and is free to photograph.

label: Historical Museum

notes: Museum of Cretan history from Byzantine times, near the waterfront.

text.description: The Historical Museum of Crete stands in Heraklion and tells the story of the island from the 4th century AD up to the Second World War. It began in 1953, when the Society of Cretan Historical Studies founded it in the former home of Minos Kalokairinos, and it has since grown with a modern wing. For a phone photographer, the appeal is a clear view of the museum building, which has a modern wing added to its original premises. Inside, the collections include icons, coins, jewellery, manuscripts and a reconstructed Cretan rural home. There are also two paintings by El Greco, his only works in Crete, and a 4×4 metre mock-up of mid-17th century Chandax, as Heraklion was then known under Venetian rule. The Nikos Kazantzakis Collection is here too. From the outside, the best photo is a straightforward view of the building front, taken from the phone icon on the map. Keep your phone level and use the gridlines so the walls and roofline stay straight. Step back as far as is comfortable and include a little of the street or sky for context. Photography rules inside museums vary and can change, so check the official site before you go and ask staff before taking any pictures of the displays.
text.geographic_location: In Heraklion, Crete. The museum is a building complex about 40 m across.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or station stops are listed for this spot. Head for the museum in Heraklion on foot, or by taxi or hired scooter if you are coming from further away. Once you reach the building, walk to the phone icon on the map, which is at the museum building itself. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the building. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street is narrow and you cannot fit the whole front in. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as doorways, windows or stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The museum is right there, so you are standing at the building itself, which is the subject of the photo. If the whole front will not fit, walk back along the street a little.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the building's vertical edges with them. Keep the phone upright and level to avoid leaning walls. Include a strip of sky and a little foreground for scale. If you want a closer shot, zoom in on doorways, windows or stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the walls keep their detail and colour.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a bright, dry time of day when the light is even on the front of the building. Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and quieter streets.

name: Venetian Loggia
label: Venetian Loggia
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Venetian Loggia' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM W305679006 (Venetian Loggia): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Elegant Venetian building on 25th August Street, now the city hall.

text.description:
The Venetian Loggia is a two-storey building with a Doric and Ionic facade, rows of arches and pale stonework. It now houses Heraklion's town hall. From the street it is a tidy, handsome frontage. The better photo, though, is inside. Visitors say the courtyard, with its arched ground-floor arcade, frames a square of open sky, and reviewers call that their favourite shot of the building. It is also quieter than the street side.

Stand in the courtyard and look up. The old walls form a frame around the sky, and the arches repeat on either side, which gives a phone photo a clear, balanced shape. Back on the street, the facade works best when you step back and tilt the phone slightly upwards, so the arches and stonework stay in view.

Because this is the town hall, the courtyard and interior are not always open. One visitor account says the courtyard is free to enter, while another says the rear area is still used as offices. The site has also been listed as temporarily closed, so check current status before you go. The exact building date is best checked on the day, so it is safest not to quote one on a caption. If the courtyard is shut, the street facade is still worth a few frames. Take one wide shot of the whole front, then one closer shot of the arches.
text.geographic_location: The Venetian Loggia is in Heraklion, where it houses the town hall. The subject is the building itself.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head straight to the Venetian Loggia. The phone icon on the map is at the building itself, so there is no extra walk once you arrive. Look for the arched stone facade. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) inside the courtyard to take in the arches and the sky together. Use the default lens (1x) for the street facade. If you can't get far enough back, the telephoto (2x or more) lets you pick out the arches and stonework from where you stand.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From there the photo shows the arched courtyard with the sky visible through its open top.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone level, then tilt it gently upwards so the courtyard walls make a frame around the sky. Switch on gridlines so the arches and walls stay straight. If the courtyard is closed, the alternative is the street facade: step back and frame the two storeys of arches and stonework from below.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the wall or arch to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky doesn't wash out to plain white. Keep the phone steady and take two or three frames to be sure one is sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: No best time is given for this spot. As a general phone tip, take a quick test frame and check how the sky looks on the screen before you settle on your shot.

text.access_note: The Loggia houses the town hall, so the courtyard and interior are not always open and may be closed temporarily: check current opening status before you go.

name: Agios Titos Church
label: Agios Titos Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Agios Titos Church' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/91031227: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Saint Titus Church' (52 m across).
notes: Historic church on the edge of Venizelou Square.

text.description: Agios Titos Church (the Cathedral of Saint Titus) is a Greek Orthodox church in the city of Heraklion, and its history shows in its looks. The present building went up from 1869 as a mosque, the Yeni Cami or 'New Mosque', after an earthquake in 1856 destroyed the mosque that stood here before. It became a Christian church in 1925 and the minaret was taken down. It was made a cathedral of the archdiocese of Crete in 2013. The result is an eclectic, square building topped with a dome, with strong vertical lines on the outside and a stone-carved apse at the top. The south side is the quiet one to photograph. Its Ottoman-style windows and dome sit against palm trees, which give the church an almost Near Eastern look and make a pleasing change from the usual front view. The front, with its open square, is the easy alternative if you want the whole building and dome in one frame. Both work well on a phone because the church is large and clearly shaped, so you can keep the composition simple. Take a few steps back, keep the lines straight, and let the palms and dome fill the frame. It is an active place of worship, so be discreet and respectful while you shoot.
text.geographic_location: Agios Titos Church stands in the city of Heraklion on Crete.
text.directions_text: Head for the centre of Heraklion and look for Agios Titos Church. The phone icon on the map marks the middle of the church outline. Once you are at the church, walk round to its south side for the view with the palms. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the south side with its windows, dome and palms. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and the dome is being cut off, and use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the dome and windows.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Walk round to the south side of the church for the south façade, with its Ottoman-style windows and dome against the palm trees. It is a quieter view than the front. If you want the main façade and dome framed by the open square instead, use that as your second shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the church walls with the vertical lines so the building does not lean. Let the palm fronds frame one side and keep the dome near the top third. For the alternative view, go round to the front and use the open square to show the dome and main façade together.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky stays blue and the dome keeps its detail. If you are shooting upwards, hold the phone level and step back rather than tilting it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually suits the stonework best. Midday sun can be harsh on the pale walls, so take a quick look at the shot and adjust the exposure.

text.access_note: The church is an active place of worship: photographing the outside is fine, but dress modestly, be discreet and do not use flash inside; rules for interior photos may vary, so check on site or with the official church website before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually suits pale stonework better than harsh midday sun.

name: Martinengo Bastion
label: Martinengo Bastion
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Martinengo Bastion (top, at the Kazantzakis tomb)' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM R5249771 (Martinego Bastion): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Venetian bastion with the tomb of writer Nikos Kazantzakis and wide views.

text.description:
Martinengo Bastion is a bastion on the Venetian walls in Heraklion, and its top is the best place in the city to take a wide photo. Several guides call it the highest point of the walls. From up there the old town, the Venetian harbour and the sea spread out to the north. The Kazantzakis tomb stands in the foreground, which gives your photo something solid to anchor the view.

The phone icon on the map is at the top of the bastion, by the tomb, so you can take the photo from the spot itself. Face north for the classic shot: tomb in the lower part of the frame, rooftops and harbour beyond, sea and sky behind. Guides say photographing the tomb is generally allowed, but be quiet and respectful around it.

For a different picture, try the Makasi gate under the bastion. It gives a close, lower view of the stone walls and the archway rising above the gate, and it is usually a quieter spot than the top of the wall. Treat it as a second option.

The views are at their best in early morning or late afternoon, when the light is particularly beautiful. Take your time at the edge of the wall, keep a firm grip on your phone, and watch your footing on uneven ground.
text.geographic_location: Martinengo Bastion is part of the Venetian walls around Heraklion's old town. It stands above the town, with the old streets, the harbour and the sea lying to the north.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops nearby. Vehicles may be able to get part of the way up, but construction can make the approach difficult, so check current conditions. The top is usually reached on foot along the walls walk, so allow a little extra time to walk up from wherever you are dropped off. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the tomb with the town behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) when you want more of the harbour and sea. A 2x zoom, if your phone has it, helps pick out details such as the harbour or the roofs.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Look north: Heraklion's old town, the Venetian harbour and the sea spread out below, with the Kazantzakis tomb in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper third line, with the tomb in the lower part of the frame. Keep the phone level so the sea line stays straight. For a quieter alternative, take a close, lower shot of the stone walls and archway at the Makasi gate under the bastion.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sea or sky to set focus and exposure, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour. Try panorama mode, moving slowly, for the sweep from old town to harbour. Keep people out of the edges of a panorama, as they can look distorted.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is particularly beautiful and the views are at their best.

text.access_note: The site may be open 24 hours, so check current opening conditions locally before you go, and check current conditions for getting up to the bastion.
extra_tips: Keep a firm grip on your phone and watch your footing at the edge of the walls, as the ground can be uneven and there may be drops.
People moving during a panorama can look distorted in the final image.
Lowering the exposure slightly helps keep sky colour in a bright scene.

name: Saint Minas Cathedral
label: Agios Minas Cathedral
camera_source: Commons cluster (1 photos), weak. Moved 6 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 30 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/175344883: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Saint Menus Cathedral' (62 m across).
notes: Large 19th-century cathedral, patron church of the city.

text.description:
Saint Minas Cathedral is the seat of the Archbishop of Crete and the patron church of Heraklion, dedicated to Saint Menas, the city's patron saint. It is the largest cathedral on Crete and one of the largest in Greece, so it is easy to spot among the buildings around it. It is also a good subject for a phone. The cruciform shape, the central dome on its high base and the two bell towers at the eastern corners give you strong lines and a clear outline to build a photo around.

The foundation stone was laid in 1862 to a design by Athanasios Moussis. Building stopped during the Cretan Revolution of 1866–1869, started again in 1883 and was finished in 1895. The outside measures about 43 metres by 29.5 metres. A much smaller church of Agios Minas, built in 1735, still stands close by, and locals call it the little Agios Minas. It makes a pleasing second photo of the old and new churches in the same area.

For your photos, begin with a wide view of the whole building. Then move closer for details such as the dome, the towers and the stonework. If people are walking across the frame, wait a moment for a gap. Look for a clean view of the dome and towers together, because that is the picture that says 'cathedral' at a glance. If you go inside, be quiet and respectful, and check the official site before you go to see whether photography is allowed.
text.geographic_location: Saint Minas Cathedral is in Heraklion, on the island of Crete. The little church of Agios Minas, the older church of the same name, stands close by.
text.directions_text: No public transport stops are listed for this spot, so ask for Saint Minas Cathedral (Agios Minas) in Heraklion. It is about 1 minute on foot from the cathedral's centre, 48 metres to the west of it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole cathedral in, as you will be quite close to a large building. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the dome and the bell towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plateia Agiou Mina (large paved square in front of the main (west) facade). The full cathedral facade with its two square bell towers and dome, framed by the open paved square. The two bell towers stand at its eastern corners, so from this side they sit at the far end of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the vertical lines of the towers upright. Put the dome near the centre, or on one of the upper grid lines, and leave a little sky above it. For a second picture, move in and use the telephoto lens on the dome or a tower. If you have time, walk to the little Agios Minas close by and photograph the two churches as a pair.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little. This stops the pale stonework and sky from washing out. Hold the phone straight, level and still, so the tall lines don't lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when the light is softer and it is usually less busy. Avoid the middle of the day, when the light is flat and harsh.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship, so dress modestly and be respectful inside, and check the official site before you go for any visiting rules.
claims_not_in_sources: From the stand-here point the cathedral is large enough that the ultra-wide (0.5x) lens helps to fit it in.
Early morning and late afternoon give softer light and usually fewer people than midday.
Modest dress and quiet behaviour are expected inside a Greek Orthodox cathedral, and photography rules inside may vary.

name: Venetian Harbour of Heraklion
label: Venetian Harbour
pin_note: Position from OSM W377197118 (Venetian Harbour): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: The old port with the Venetian arsenals and fishing boats.

text.description:
The Venetian Harbour is the old harbour area of Heraklion, on the waterfront in the city centre. Harbour views tend to suit a phone camera well because the scene is usually open and easy to read. You are likely to see water, boats and buildings. You don't need to find a clever angle. A simple, level frame from the right spot often looks good.

From there, start with the default lens (1x) and keep the horizon level if you can see one. If you want a few boats or the harbour edge as the main subject, step closer and zoom in a little. Look along edges, boats and buildings as well as straight ahead, as lines like these give the picture depth.

Take a few frames at different distances, one wide and one closer, and choose later. Wipe your lens before you start, as pockets and bags leave marks that show up as haze. Boats and people move, so take several shots and keep the sharpest. Follow any local signs about access restrictions.
text.geographic_location: On the Heraklion waterfront, in the old harbour area of the city centre, where the town meets the sea.
text.directions_text: The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the harbour. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit in more of the scene and sky. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out boats or details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Koules Fortress (top ramparts (roof walkway) of the fortress, looking out over the harbour). The whole harbour basin with its moored boats, the fortress wall in the foreground, and the sea and town beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the horizon up with one of them. Put any water or quay in the foreground and let the harbour fill the middle of the frame. Take one wide shot, then one closer shot with a zoom lens.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or water to set the focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly to keep the sky from washing out. Try a Live Photo if boats or people are moving.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is usually kinder on water and buildings than midday sun. Check the weather and see how the light looks when you arrive.

text.access_note: Follow any local signs about access rules or restrictions.
claims_not_in_sources: The Venetian Harbour is on the Heraklion waterfront in the city centre.
The scene is likely to include water, boats and buildings.
Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters water and buildings more than midday sun.
Access to some parts of the harbour area may be restricted, so local signs should be followed.

name: Saint Mark's Basilica
label: Saint Mark's Basilica
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Πλατεία Ελευθερίου Βενιζέλου' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Πλατεία Ελευθερίου Βενιζέλου' (relation/12119943): middle (100 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/228646533: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Basilica of Saint Mark' (55 m across).
notes: Reconstructed Venetian church beside Lions Square.

text.description:
Saint Mark's Basilica stands in the centre of Heraklion, on Eleftheriou Venizelou Square, a short step from the Morosini (Lions) Fountain. The Venetians built it in 1239 in the Gothic style. It was later a mosque, from the Ottoman conquest in 1669 until 1915, and after restoration work that began in 1956 it became a public art gallery. It is one of the few former Roman Catholic churches still standing in Crete. A minaret and a bell tower once stood here, but neither survives.

It photographs well because the front is easy to read: a portico on the western side and a row of arches, with the fountain close by to give the picture a foreground. The calm stone façade works well against the busy square around it.

From the square the building is straight ahead to the east. Start with a wide view that shows the portico, the arches and a bit of the fountain, then move in for details. A calmer alternative is to walk along 25ης Αυγούστου (25th August Street) for a side-on, angled view of the façade. For a close-up, the carved stone doorway is worth a few frames. The square is a busy public space, so take a moment to let people walk out of your shot. If you want to photograph inside, check the rules at the official site first.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Heraklion, on Eleftheriou Venizelou Square, directly across from the Morosini (Lions) Fountain.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, tram or railway stops nearby, so head for the centre of Heraklion by taxi or hired scooter and ask for the Lions Fountain square (Eleftheriou Venizelou Square). The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the portico and arches with the fountain at the edge of the frame. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the square is crowded and you cannot step back. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the carved doorway and stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Πλατεία Ελευθερίου Βενιζέλου (directly opposite the Morosini (Lions) Fountain, on the square's basilica side). The basilica's front portico and arched facade, with the Lions Fountain close by to frame the building. On the basilica side and directly opposite the Morosini (Lions) Fountain, with the basilica to the east. From here you see the front portico and arched façade, with the fountain close by to frame the building. This is the standard postcard angle. If the square is too busy, 25ης Αυγούστου gives a side-on or angled view of the façade.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the portico on one of the vertical lines, with the fountain in the lower corner as a foreground. Keep the phone level so the arches do not lean. For a different shot, walk along 25ης Αυγούστου and frame the façade at an angle, or move close to the doorway and use the telephoto for the carved details.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone façade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its colour and texture. Wait for a gap in the crowd before you press the shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning should mean fewer people in the square, and the façade is west-facing, so it should catch the light in the late afternoon and evening. Check the sky on the day.

text.access_note: The basilica is now an art gallery and the square in front is an open public space; check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements and for the rules on photography inside.
claims_not_in_sources: The basilica's façade faces west, so it is likely to catch the light in the late afternoon and evening (inferred from the portico being on the western façade).
Early morning is likely to be quieter in the square than later in the day.
The square is a busy public space with people passing through.
